newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian churches back Aborigines in land fight.
newsitem.headline: Australian churches back Aborigines in land fight.

text.p: Australian church leaders threw their weight behind the country's Aborigines on Thursday in a dispute over whether indigenous people can claim rights over long-held farming land.

The Australian High Court decided last year that "pastoral leases" granted to farmers and graziers over the past 200 years did not necessarily take precedence over "native title" rights formally granted to Aborigines four years ago.
Its ruling, known as "the Wik decision", has caused uncertainty among farmers and mining companies who operate in rural areas.
Prime Minister John Howard warned on Wednesday that 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 sq miles) of land was "potentially claimable" by Aborigines.
But church leaders on Thursday warned Howard that it would be a mistake to extinguish native title on pastoral lease land and any solution must respect Aboriginal rights.
"If there's forced extinguishment we would consider that morally wrong because it's discrimination," said Bishop Kevin Manning, spokesman for the Australian Catholic Bishops' Conference.

"Any expansion of rights of pastoralists must be negotiated with the traditional owners," added the Uniting Church, the country's third-largest Christian denomination, in a letter which the church sent to Howard on Thursday.

Howard has described the Wik issue as the most difficult challenge he faces as prime minister. The dispute has also provoked a split between his own Liberal party and the junior party in his coalition governnment, the National party.
National party leader and deputy prime minister Tim Fischer has pushed Howard to extinguish native title.

Howard has hinted that he might take a tough stance, but is still looking for a compromise solution in which native title rights could coexist with pastoral leases without threatening the future of farmers.
Bishop Manning said the Catholic church supported a compromise solution.
"We recognise the need that all parties have for security of title," he said. "It would be wrong and futile to try to obtain such security by forcibly extinguishing native title to lands."
